strengths: Addresses an important and realistic NLP challenge: fine-grained, token-level semantic difference recognition across document-level cross-lingual texts, moving beyond artificial sentence concatenations and machine-translated synthetic benchmarks.

The paper is well-situated within existing literature (e.g., iSTS-RSD, MQM, word-level quality estimation) and demonstrates convincingly that models trained on synthetically augmented data fail to generalize to naturalistic document-level data.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing a diverse suite of encoders (XLM-R, LaBSE, ModernBERT, EuroBERT, MmBERT, Qwen3-Embedding) and modern LLMs (Llama-3.1, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) across unsupervised, few-shot prompting, and fine-tuning setups.
Transparent and thorough analysis of LLM failure modes, including JSON decoding/length mismatches, context degradation towards document ends, and runtime efficiency.
weaknesses: Low inter-annotator agreement on span identification: Mean Intersection-over-Union (IoU) is quite low (10.22%–11.17% for EN–DE, 24%–30% for EN–FR, and 32%–44% for EN–IT). As shown in Appendix A.4, model evaluation correlations vary widely depending on which annotator's annotations are evaluated against, raising concerns about benchmark stability.

Modest dataset scale and coverage: The benchmark contains 224 document pairs across only three closely related high-resource European languages (German, French, Italian) paired with English, limiting claims about broader cross-lingual generalizability.

The LLM prompting formulation requires the model to autoregressively output a list of every token paired with a numeric label for long documents (up to thousands of tokens), a setup known to severely strain autoregressive decoders. Comparing this against span-based extraction or chunked/sliding-window prompting would provide a fairer assessment of LLM capabilities.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem: semantic difference recognition (RSD) across natural, cross-lingual documents, moving significantly beyond previous synthetic sentence-level augmentations.
Provides a valuable new human-annotated benchmark (SwissGov-RSD) covering 224 multi-parallel documents across English-German, English-French, and English-Italian from official administrative domains.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning multiple model paradigms: unsupervised token alignment (DiffAlign with diverse encoders), proprietary and open-weights LLMs (including reasoning models), and fine-tuned encoders/LLMs.

Clear, impactful empirical finding: demonstrates a dramatic performance collapse when transitioning from synthetic benchmarks (iSTS-RSD) to naturalistic documents (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini dropping from ~80 to ~1-5 Spearman correlation), showing that synthetic data does not reliably reflect real-world document divergence.
Strong documentation of annotation procedures, compensations, detailed guidelines, and transparent reporting of annotator agreement and error failure rates.
weaknesses: Low inter-annotator agreement at the span level, especially for English-German (IoU ~10-11%, F1 ~17-18%). While the authors contextualize this with reference to human MT error span evaluation, such low span overlap indicates high task subjectivity and potentially fuzzy span boundary definitions.

The dataset is evaluated purely in a zero-shot / out-of-domain transfer setup; no train/test split or in-domain fine-tuning baseline is established on SwissGov-RSD itself, leaving open whether supervised modeling on natural data can bridge the gap.

The evaluation relies predominantly on token-level rank correlation metrics (Spearman and Kendall tau-b) over highly skewed distributions where 85-90% of tokens are 0. Standard sequence labeling or detection metrics (e.g., token/span-level Precision, Recall, F1, or PR-AUC) would provide a clearer operational assessment.

LLM evaluation methodology via monolithic JSON output generation is prone to truncation and alignment errors over long documents (up to 2,500+ tokens), which may penalize generative models compared to sentence-by-sentence or chunked prompting strategies.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic gap in semantic similarity and text comparison by moving beyond synthetically augmented sentence-level data to naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual semantic difference recognition.
The dataset creation process is well-documented, featuring clear multi-stage annotation guidelines, trial calibration phases, and fair compensation for annotators.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation comparing a broad suite of paradigms, including unsupervised embedding alignment (DiffAlign), modern long-context encoders, few-shot prompting of major proprietary and open LLMs (including reasoning models), and fine-tuned models.

The core finding is striking and consequential: models that appear to solve synthetic benchmarks (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini scoring ~80 Spearman correlation on iSTS-RSD) completely collapse when evaluated on naturalistic governmental documents (dropping to near zero), demonstrating severe overfitting to synthetic augmentation patterns.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement at the span level is low, particularly for EN–DE (mean IoU of ~10–11% and F1 of ~17–18%), indicating substantial subjectivity in span boundary selection and differing annotator strategies regarding omissions versus stylistic differences.
The benchmark scale and linguistic diversity are relatively limited: 224 document pairs restricted to English paired with three closely related European languages (German, French, Italian).

Model performance on SwissGov-RSD is uniformly near-floor (Spearman correlations rarely exceeding 0.20–0.25). While this clearly exposes the dataset's difficulty, the paper does not propose or validate any effective methodological solution or modeling paradigm to bridge this gap.

Several model evaluations on SwissGov-RSD are omitted (e.g., fine-tuned Llama-3.1 8B, DeepSeek-R1, and o3-mini in Table 3) due to computational constraints, leaving gaps in comparing the latest reasoning and open-weights models on the newly introduced resource.

strengths: High-value naturalistic dataset: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level recognition of semantic differences (RSD), moving beyond synthetic sentence-concatenation benchmarks (like iSTS-RSD).

Rigorous annotation process: Employs a structured two-phase annotation methodology (trial with manual feedback and main phase) using trained computational linguistics students who were fairly compensated ($35/h), with detailed inter-annotator agreement analyses (IoU, F1, Spearman across exact and fuzzy matches).

Extensive and up-to-date empirical evaluation: Evaluates a wide spectrum of models—unsupervised encoder representations (including recent architectures like ModernBERT, EuroBERT, MmBERT, and Qwen3-Embedding), modern LLMs with prompting and reasoning (GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, LLaMA-3.1), and fine-tuned models utilizing cross-lingual label projection.

Insightful diagnostic findings: Unveils a dramatic performance collapse across all model families when transferring from synthetic benchmarks to real-world documents (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini dropping from ~80 to ~1–5 Spearman correlation), revealing substantial vulnerabilities in current data augmentation and long-context alignment capabilities.

Clear writing, actionable error analysis, and open-source contribution: The paper is well-structured, analyzes positional degradation and LLM length-mismatch failures in detail, and commits to releasing code and datasets under permissive licensing.
weaknesses: Linguistic and domain diversity is constrained: The dataset is restricted to Swiss administrative texts and three closely related European languages paired with English (EN–DE, EN–FR, EN–IT), leaving non-Latin scripts, low-resource, and typologically diverse languages unexplored in this naturalistic setting.

Relatively low inter-annotator agreement: Raw token-level Spearman correlation between annotators is moderate (43.61 to 65.09) with low span IoU (24–43%), reflecting inherent subjectivity in span boundary definition (word-level vs. phrasal units) that partly limits the upper-bound reliability of token-level gold labels.

LLM formulation induces structural failures: Evaluating LLMs by autoregressively predicting token-by-token scores in JSON over inputs spanning thousands of words is known to trigger severe alignment and token count errors (up to 7.4% fail rate). Exploring span extraction or chunk-based/hierarchical prompting could have provided a fairer representation of LLM capabilities.

Limited encoder fine-tuning configurations: Fine-tuning for the regression baseline was exclusively conducted with ModernBERT-large (predominantly English-centric), while top-performing multilingual embedding encoders (e.g., XLM-R, Qwen3-Embedding) were only tested in the zero-shot/DiffAlign setting.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem: token-level semantic difference recognition in real-world, naturally occurring cross-lingual document pairs, moving beyond the synthetic sentence-concatenation setups used in prior work (e.g., iSTS-RSD).

Presents an important empirical finding: systems that perform exceptionally well on synthetic benchmarks (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini reaching ~80 Spearman on iSTS-RSD) experience severe degradation on natural documents (dropping to 1–5), exposing significant distribution and formatting transfer gaps.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across various architectures and paradigms, including unsupervised embedding alignment (DiffAlign), modern long-context encoders (ModernBERT, EuroBERT, Qwen3-Embedding), open/proprietary LLMs, reasoning models, and fine-tuned baselines.
Well-documented annotation methodology and clear supplementary material, including guidelines, prompt templates, failure rate analysis, and position-dependent performance breakdown.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is relatively low (token-level Spearman of 43.61 to 65.09, and English IoU around 24–32%), reflecting the high subjectivity and difficulty of span-level difference labeling. Only two annotators per language pair were employed, and only 25 documents were overlapped for validation, leaving some uncertainty about gold-standard consistency.

No in-domain supervised or few-shot adaptation experiment on SwissGov-RSD itself (e.g., k-fold cross-validation or train/test splitting). Because all fine-tuning was conducted on synthetic iSTS-RSD data, it remains unclear whether models fail due to an inherent inability to perform long-document cross-lingual RSD or primarily due to out-of-domain transfer and format mismatch.
The dataset is relatively modest in size (224 multi-parallel documents) and limited strictly to English paired with closely related European languages (German, French, Italian).

Evaluation relies predominantly on rank correlation (Spearman and Kendall tau-b) over heavily skewed token distributions (83–90% zeros). Complementary span-level detection metrics (e.g., span-level Precision, Recall, and F1 at various IoU thresholds) would provide a clearer operational picture of practical system utility.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem: prior work on cross-lingual recognition of semantic differences (RSD) relied almost exclusively on synthetically concatenated sentence pairs (iSTS-RSD), leaving naturalistic, document-level performance unmeasured.

Careful data collection and annotation methodology: SwissGov-RSD provides 224 multi-parallel documents (~170k–195k tokens per language pair) across English-German, English-French, and English-Italian with detailed guidelines, fair annotator compensation, and a thorough inter-annotator validation study reporting IoU, F1, and rank correlation.

Extensive and diverse benchmarking: the paper evaluates unsupervised encoder-based difference alignment (XLM-R, LaBSE, EuroBERT, Qwen3-Embedding), few-shot prompting with contemporary LLMs (GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.1-405B, reasoning models like o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1), and fine-tuned models utilizing LLM-based label projection.

Compelling and cautionary empirical findings: demonstrates that systems achieving seemingly high performance on synthetic benchmarks (~80 Spearman rho) experience severe degradation on naturalistic document data (dropping to 1–25 rho), highlighting significant vulnerabilities in synthetic evaluation pipelines and current LLM-based structured token labeling.
weaknesses: Modest dataset scale and language diversity: although token counts are sizable, the corpus contains only 224 document pairs and is limited to English paired with three closely related Western European languages (German, French, Italian), leaving typologically diverse languages and scripts unexplored.

Moderate inter-annotator agreement: span overlap statistics are relatively low (mean English IoU ~24–32% and token-level Spearman correlation 43.6–65.1), indicating substantial annotator subjectivity in span boundary definition and difference severity, despite being consistent with related token-level error annotation tasks.

Prompting and modeling design for LLMs on long documents: querying LLMs to output entire sequences as JSON token-by-token frequently causes formatting failures, truncations, and length mismatches on longer texts; exploring windowed/chunked prompting or span extraction formats could have provided a stronger, fairer LLM baseline.

Analysis of failure modes could be deepened: while the paper attributes the performance gap largely to length, domain shifts, and label distribution skew, further empirical breakdown by specific phenomena (e.g., omission/addition vs. nuanced semantic divergence, or localized vs. global structural shifts) would provide clearer diagnostic value.
